explain.say: In Japan, people often bow to say hello. In Brazil, friends may kiss on the cheek. In India, many say namaste with joined hands. Same job, different ways! That shared way of life is called culture. Look at the board: culture has two kinds of parts.

explain.say: See the first group, easy to see? Food like jollof rice or tacos, clothes like a sari or a kimono, festivals, music and language. These are the parts you notice straight away when you visit somewhere new. What is a food from your culture?

explain.say: Now look at the second group, hidden below. Values, which means what people think is important, plus manners, ideas about time and family roles. You cannot see these, but they shape everything. Is it polite to arrive early or right on time where you live?

explain.say: People often compare culture to an iceberg. The small top is what you see; the huge part under the water is hidden. Look at both groups together. Most surprises between cultures come from the hidden part, like whether you look an elder in the eye. Which group do you think is bigger?

explain.say: So culture is the whole way of life a group shares and passes on, the seen and the unseen. And everyone has culture, including you, often more than one! Great job! Challenge: ask an older relative about one hidden rule from your family's culture.

faq.a: Culture is the shared way of life of a group of people: their food, language, clothes, festivals, manners, values and beliefs, passed from older people to younger ones.

faq.q: What parts of culture can you see?
faq.a: Visible parts include food, clothes, festivals, music, dance, art and language. These are what you notice first when you visit a new place.
asks: Tell me about easy to see

faq.q: What are the hidden parts of culture?
faq.a: Hidden parts include values, manners, ideas about time, how families work, how people show respect, and beliefs. You cannot see them, but they guide how people act.

It is a way of picturing culture: like an iceberg, only a small part shows above the water, while the larger part, values and beliefs, is hidden underneath. The idea is often linked to anthropologist Edward T. Hall.
asks: Why is culture like an iceberg?

faq.q: Can a person belong to more than one culture?
faq.a: Yes. Many people share the culture of their family, their country, their religion and their friends at once, and mix them in their own way.
asks: Can you be part of many cultures?

facts: More than 7,000 languages are spoken in the world today (Ethnologue).
UNESCO lists hundreds of traditions, such as Indian yoga and Mexican Day of the Dead, as Intangible Cultural Heritage.
